doc.title: Writing Tests
doc.paragraph: This section goes over how to add tests that afwdev test will run. Tests live with the source they cover, in each source directory's tests folder.

section.title: Where Tests Live
section.paragraph: Under each source directory:
section.code: src/<srcdir>/tests/ some_group/ # related tests (one or more files) foo.as bar.as afw.conf # optional; used when the group needs conf objects/ # optional fixtures config.py # optional Tags, Environment, before/after hooks environments/ # optional shared fixtures (named; see config.py) models/ afw.conf …
section.paragraph: The afwdev test command looks under src/*/tests/. You can limit what it runs with --srcdir-pattern and --test-pattern. Related tests that share conf or data should stay in the same directory. There is also a short note in src/afw/tests/README.md.

section.title: Running Tests
section.paragraph: After you change source or generated files, build from the package root with ./afwdev build --cdev. The ./afwdev in the package root is the one to use for a build, since the build may install a new afwdev. After that, the afwdev on your PATH is current, and you use it for test, validate, and similar commands.

A failing test always prints a one-line reason; under valgrind it also includes the kind of error and the top frames. When you need more, pass --error-detail to see the source, what was expected next to what came back, and a short backtrace. For everything, including passing tests and the full valgrind output, put the global option before the command: afwdev --debug test ….
section.code:
# From the package root, after source or generate changes ./afwdev build --cdev -j
# Run tests (installed afw / afwfcgi on PATH) afwdev test -j afwdev test --srcdir-pattern afw --test-pattern 'rql/.*' afwdev test --list --test-pattern smoke # A real --test-pattern shows passing cases (no --show-all needed) # Fail-only extras (source, expect/result, short backtrace); not --debug afwdev test --error-detail --test-pattern 'http_put' --env-mode valgrind -j
section.paragraph: Each test file gets a line with how long it took and the most memory one case used. xctx is what the code asked for, and chunk is what the memory region actually mapped. At the end of the run, a summary tells you how it went:
section.code: src/afw/tests/language/script/try.as (33ms, max 743,824 xctx, 917,504 chunk) PASS Additional try tests, some accessing error object and data. ... Source Dirs: 20 passed, 20 total Tests: 38 passed, 38 total Elapsed: 0.3s CPU: 0.5s Memory: max 743,824 xctx, 917,504 chunk Out of family: 0 (memory, 1 matched tests) vs baseline a96e2fe68 (...) History: /root/.afw/test-history/2026-10-15T212758614Z-afw.json Run: /tmp/afwdev-runs/1015-212758-afw (keeps the last 10 afw runs and 10 failed)

list.item: Tests counts cases that passed, failed, and were skipped. A run that sent fuzz requests adds a Fuzz line.
Out of family is the number of tests that used noticeably more memory than in the run they are compared with (see Test History and Baselines). It is something to look at, not a failure.
History is the file this run was saved to, and Run is its work directory.
When something failed, the summary lists each failing file with its reason, a Re-run line with the command to run just those, and Failures, the failures.log in the run directory with the details.

row.column: Run test groups in parallel.
-p, --srcdir-pattern
Only source directories whose name matches.
Only test files whose path or name matches; passing cases are shown too.
Only groups whose Tags in config.py match the regular expression.
Show what would run, without running it.
-b [N], --bail
Stop after the first failed test, or after N.
Show passing tests too; normally only failures are shown.
More detail on each failure.
Run the tests again each time a file changes.
How tests run: afw, valgrind, asan, tsan, ... (see How afwdev test Runs Tests).
Test the cmake build tree instead of the install.
-T, --tests-path
Run the tests in this directory tree instead of the package's tests folders, such as a leaf under src/afw/tests-extra/.
Run the JavaScript and admin app tests instead.
Where run directories go; /tmp unless you say otherwise.

section.paragraph: Before you open a pull request, the Contributing chapter lists the runs to make for each kind of change. A change that reaches C needs the valgrind and AddressSanitizer runs as well as the normal one.

section.title: Kinds of Tests
section.paragraph: The following table describes the kinds of tests the runner understands:

row.column: Adaptive test script (.as, --syntax test_script)
This is the usual kind of test. Use it for language, functions, and adapters. You may include an afw.conf if the test needs one.
Python (.py with run())
Use a Python test when you need to control the process, read environment values, or call APIs that are not easy to use from Adaptive Script.
C probe (*_probe.c plus a thin .py)
Use a C probe when Adaptive Script cannot reach the hole. See C Probes below.
A file whose name starts with commands_ and ends with .txt runs a sequence of commands.
Orchestrated test
A directory with an orchestration.yaml file. Use it for more than one request, or when you need a long-running afwfcgi. See Orchestrated Tests below.

section.paragraph: You will usually want to write an Adaptive test script, unless you need a separate process, your own server, Python APIs, or a C probe.

section.title: C Probes
section.paragraph: Prefer an Adaptive test script. Write a C probe only when script cannot reach the code under test: a wrapping size_t, a second implementation of an interface that literals never use, a hand-set afw_utf8_t, helpers that need a live directory to go through the adapter, and similar holes. The .c is not part of the cmake library build and is not a cmake test target. It compiles against the installed libafw at test time.

Start with afwdev prime-test-c-probe <path>. The path is relative to the current directory or absolute, and must be a new leaf under tests/ or tests-extra/ (for example tests/hole from an extension srcdir, or src/myext/tests/advanced/hole from the package root). That writes the closet pair. Fill the marked blocks in the .c and the case list in the .py. Then afwdev test --test-pattern 'hole', or afwdev test -T <path> for a tests-extra leaf. The closet itself is src/afw_dev/_resources/closet/c_probe/ if you need to copy by hand.

Check in a *_probe.c next to a thin Python run() that calls run_c_probe() from _afwdev.test.c_probe. The helper compiles the probe once and runs each named case. The probe takes the case name as argv[1] and exits 0 on pass.

Extra libraries go in libraries. The LDAP filter probe uses libraries=("afwldap", "afw"). Headers and libraries come from the install prefix, or from AFW_INCLUDE_DIR and AFW_LIB_DIR. Pass extra -I in extra_cflags when the probe needs a core-internal header from the source tree. Those flags are searched before the install include directory so a leftover *_internal.h in the prefix cannot win.
Live examples (after you have the closet copy): src/afw/tests/advanced/pool_alloc/, array_view_index/, utf8_icu_bound/, and src/afw_ldap/tests/ldap_filter/.

afwdev test --env-mode valgrind still wraps Adaptive scripts with the afw CLI. The same mode also wraps C probes: the helper runs each case under valgrind with the suite suppressions (valgrind.suppress). Those suppressions cover known libunwind noise inside afw_os_backtrace when a probe throws. That is not an overread in the code under test. A standalone valgrind on the compiled probe, without that file, can still report that noise. Judge a probe by its exit code, and by the helper's valgrind wrap when you want memory checking. A valgrind fail prints kind and the top stack frames. Pass --error-detail for source, expected vs result, and a short backtrace on any fail. Full valgrind XML stays --debug. -j keeps each group together. The UTF-8 and error-struct side of a throw is a separate issue from this recipe.

section.title: Adaptive Test Scripts
section.paragraph: Most tests are Adaptive test scripts. These are .as files compiled with --syntax test_script. A file starts with a shebang that names afw and test_script, then one or more cases described by //? metadata lines.

The shebang must mention afw and test_script, as above or as afw --syntax test_script. Metadata lines start with //?. Common keys are test, description, expect, source, and skip. Failures are reported for each test: case.

Multi-line values use //? key: ... and then the text on the following lines until the next //?, or the end of the file. That form keeps the text as you wrote it, including newlines. A blank line before the next //? is the usual way to keep a final newline on the last content line.

File values use //? key: <<< relative/path, with the path relative to the directory of the .as file. The file contents become the key's value exactly, with no trimming. Paths must be relative and must not contain .. segments. This is useful for long expects or sources. A value that starts with <<< is always this form, so do not begin a description with those characters. After //? source: ... or //? source: <<< …, the body is the multi-line or file form above.

The expect key is usually Adaptive source for the return value you want, for instance 0, true, "ok", "…"anyURI, or undefined. It is not free text. The runner compiles and evaluates that source and compares it to the result of the case. A <<< file for expect must contain that Adaptive source. For instance, put quotes around "hello" if you want a string return value.

Two reserved tokens are not Adaptive values. The token success means the case compiled and ran without throwing. The result is ignored. The token error, or error: followed by a message, means the case should throw.

Optional keys expect-stdout and expect-stderr check the text written to the Adaptive stdout and stderr streams during the case, for instance by print, println, or stream writes. These values are literal strings, not Adaptive source. They use the same forms as other keys: same-line trim, ..., or <<<. Comparison is exact utf-8. Use a hyphen in the key name. Do not put a colon inside the name. expect:stdout is wrong, because : separates the key from the value. When these keys are present, the output is captured so it does not get mixed in with the test result. If you omit the key, that stream is ignored.

If the script needs adapters or other conf, put afw.conf in the same directory, or use a shared tests/environments/<name>/ and set Environment in config.py. The default --env-mode afw runs afw with that conf when the group provides it. Keep extra files small. The runner copies the group's files into a temporary work directory.
A group may define:

list.item: Tags — a list of strings. afwdev test --tags with a regular expression selects groups.
Environment — the name of a directory under tests/environments/.
before_all, after_all, before_each, and after_each — hooks.

section.paragraph: See existing config.py files under src/afw/tests/ for patterns. The easiest way to start is to copy an existing test and change it. For instance, look at src/afw/tests/language/script/try.as and src/afw/tests/compiler/test_script_file_value/.

section.title: How afwdev test Runs Tests
section.paragraph: The --env-mode option chooses how each test is run:

row.column: afw (default)
Runs .as files with a subprocess afw. Orchestrated tests start their own afwfcgi.

Runs .as files under valgrind. C probes compiled by run_c_probe() are also wrapped. Orchestrated tests wrap afwfcgi when that is supported. A fail prints valgrind kind and the top stack frames. --error-detail adds source/expect/backtrace. The full valgrind XML is shown with afwdev --debug test. -j prints each test group as one block.

Runs the suite against the AddressSanitizer + UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer build from ./afwdev build --cdev --sanitize address (build/asan/cmake/, never installed). Python tests, C probes and orchestrated afwfcgi use the same build. Any sanitizer report fails the process that hit it, and a fail shows the report line and the top stack frames. Opt-in: about 6 minutes for the suite.

Runs the suite the same way against the ThreadSanitizer + UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer build from ./afwdev build --cdev --sanitize thread (build/tsan/cmake/, never installed). Races need more than one thread, so reports come from the multi-threaded orchestrated afwfcgi tests. The stack limit is capped at 4 MiB for the run. Opt-in: about 80 seconds for the suite.

Replays compatible .as files against a running stack. The default URL is http://localhost:8080/afw. Tests with their own afw.conf are skipped. Orchestrated tests are also skipped, because their conf does not apply to the running process.
A local Python Session and eval_script for .as files.

section.paragraph: Some files always use their own runner. A .py file uses the Python runner. A commands_*.txt file uses the commands runner.

By default, tests run the installed afw, afwfcgi and libraries. --build-tree runs them from the cmake build tree instead (build/cmake/), so no install is needed to test. The asan mode always uses its own tree.

section.title: Orchestrated Tests
section.paragraph: Use an orchestrated test when you need a long-running afwfcgi, conf that belongs to that test, more than one request, REST feeds, or an Accept header such as application/x-afw. You can also use a firehose schedule. The test is a directory that contains orchestration.yaml. See src/afw/tests-extra/README.md and the examples under src/afw/tests/advanced/.

The same keys can be used where they apply: expect, expect-stdout, expect-stderr, plus expectResponse and expectStatus for HTTP bodies, and expectHeaders (header name to expected value) for REST response headers.

Tests under src/afw/tests/ are run by afwdev test -j. Keep those short. Tests under src/afw/tests-extra/ are additional tests that you run only when you pass -T. Use that tree for longer tests, including firehose. More detail is in src/afw/tests-extra/README.md.
section.code: src/afw/tests-extra/<name>/ # or tests/<group>/ for tests in the default run orchestration.yaml # or orchestration.json (not both) afw.conf objects/ # optional fixtures tests/ or *.as # payloads (sourcePath / <<<)

version: 1 host: afwfcgi description: Short summary afwfcgi: threads: 1 timeout_s: 60 feed: # defaults for every test kind: action accept: application/json tests: - name: first sourceType: script source: | return true; expect: true - name: progressive feed: accept: application/x-afw # override default Accept only sourceType: script sourcePath: tests/to_response.as # optional schedule: sequential | parallel | firehose | repeat

list.item: A document-level feed supplies defaults. A per-test feed overrides fields.
sourceType together with source, sourcePath, or <<< path is the same idea as evaluating a test script.
expect optionally compares the JSON result of the action. Test script payloads use the inner passed flag.
schedule.firehose takes duration, concurrency, maxRequests, and fromTests for load.
This requires PyYAML and afwfcgi on PATH from an install build.

section.code: afwdev test --capture-goldens -T path/to/test # or: AFWDEV_CAPTURE_GOLDENS=1 afwdev test -T path/to/test
section.paragraph: That writes the actual response bytes to each expectResponse: <<< rel/path. Run again without capture to check them.

A test directory can declare parameters, each with a name, a default and a description, and use them wherever a value is exactly $name. You change one for a run with --set: NAME=VALUE for every test that declares it, LEAF:NAME=VALUE for one test directory, or @FILE for a YAML or JSON file of those keys. Each value takes the type of its default, and none clears it. A firehose step can also send generated requests with fuzz:. When one of them fails, the failure names the request as SEED:INDEX, and you can send just that request again:
section.code: afwdev test -T src/afw/tests-extra/fuzz-hostile --set seed=7 --set duration_s=60 afwdev test -T src/afw/tests-extra/fuzz-hostile --list # shows each parameter as a --set line afwdev test -T path/to/test --replay 1234:57 # Cut a failing request down to the smallest one that still fails the same way afwdev test -T path/to/test --replay 1234:57:shrink
section.paragraph: The details are in src/afw/tests-extra/SCHEMA.md.

section.title: Looking at a Test Server in a Browser
section.paragraph: Sometimes you want to see a change rather than test it: a new handbook page, or the admin app against a server with real adapters. The manual leaf under src/afw/tests-extra/ starts an afwfcgi with no load, and keeps it running until you stop it:

In front of the server is a small HTTP front on a free port of 127.0.0.1, which the leaf prints. It serves the built handbook under /docs/ (from build/docs), the admin app under /apps/ (from build/js/apps), and sends every other path to the leaf's afwfcgi. Opening the port's root goes to the admin app. Files are read from the build directories on each request, so after ./afwdev build --docs a reload shows the new pages. Every 30 seconds the leaf prints a line with the request count, threads, pool bytes, and RSS. Stop it with Ctrl-C, or with a POST to /stop on that port.
The configuration, objects, and a private LDAP server come from the firehose leaf, which runs the same server under load.

section.title: Test History and Baselines
section.paragraph: Each run of afwdev test is saved in a history (by default under ~/.afw/test-history/), one per --env-mode. For each test it keeps how much memory the test used and how long it took. The next run compares each test's memory with the same test in an earlier run, and marks the line of any test that used noticeably more as out of family. That mark means the test is worth a look, not that it failed. Time is kept but not compared, because a short test's time is mostly afw starting up and moves with the load on the machine. A test whose file changed since the earlier run is counted as changed, not compared, since new cases usually mean more memory.

By default the comparison is with the newest baseline from another branch that your branch contains, which is usually the gate run of the last pull request that merged. You make a baseline by adding --baseline to a full run of a mode (it is refused with --test-pattern, --srcdir-pattern or -T). --compare-to picks something else to compare with: last for the previous run, a commit hash, or a history file. --trend runs no tests and shows how the runs since then moved; give it bytes, chunk, cpu or ms to choose what to rank by.
section.code: afwdev test -j --baseline # this branch's baseline for afw mode afwdev test -j --env-mode valgrind --baseline afwdev test -j --compare-to last # compare with the previous run afwdev test --trend cpu
section.paragraph: Each run works in its own directory, afwdev-runs/<MMDD-HHMMSS>-<mode>/ under --tmpdir, with afwdev-runs/latest pointing to the newest one. Tests get their temporary files there, and a run that had a failure writes the details to failures.log in it. Each mode keeps its ten newest runs and, separately, its ten newest failed runs, so a long string of passing runs never pushes out a failure; set test_keep_runs in afwdev-settings.json to keep a different number. --clear-temps removes every run directory that no running test holds, and --clear-history deletes this mode's saved history except its baselines and other tagged runs.
For a script or CI job, --output writes a summary of the results to a file, or to standard output with -. --output-format chooses json (the default), json-compact or text:

section.title: Tips

list.item: Copy a test that is already close to what you need and change it.
Name files so --test-pattern is useful. Patterns match the file path, the file name, or the directory name of an orchestrated test.
Keep groups small. Shared conf is fine. Do not put unrelated tests in one directory if you want them to run in parallel.
After you make a change that should be tested, run afwdev test -j. Valgrind mode is slower, so save it for when you need it, such as the runs before a pull request that reaches C.
Many function and datatype scripts under tests/generated/ are generated. For new tests, add a hand-written file under a clear group name.
Put long load tests in orchestrated tests under src/afw/tests-extra/, or under other -T roots. Do not put heavy firehose tests in the default tests/ run.

section.paragraph: The orchestrated schema is described in src/afw/tests-extra/SCHEMA.md. Command help is available from afw --help (-s test_script) and afwdev test --help.
